title: Social media users' perceptions about health mis- and disinformation on social media
screen_reason: Nationally representative US survey (HINTS 6, 2022, n=3841 adult social media users) reporting the share of respondents who perceive false or misleading health information on social media on a none / a little / some / a lot scale. 'Perceived amount of misinformation in one's environment (a lot / some / none)' is explicitly in scope as RECALL, and the paper reports shares of respondents in each category as well as the dichotomised headline (82%).

estimates.measure_type: % of adult social media users who perceive 'some' or 'a lot' of the health information they see on social media to be false or misleading
estimates.value_raw: 82% (survey-weighted: some 46% [raw n 1768] + a lot 36% [raw n 1358]; none/a little 18% [raw n 715])
estimates.denominator: 3,841 US adults aged 18+ who had visited a social media site in the past year (HINTS 6, nationally representative, survey-weighted with jackknife replicate weights)
estimates.definition: A respondent counted if they answered 'some' or 'a lot' to 'How much of the health information that you see on social media do you think is false or misleading?' (categories: I do not use social media / none / a little / some / a lot; non-users coded missing)
estimates.misinfo_def: “Misinformation is false or inaccurate information, while disinformation is intentionally disseminating false or inaccurate information.”
estimates.source_quote: health information on social media. Our finding that 82% of adult social media users perceived false or misleading health information on social media is consistent with estimates from objective content analyses of social media posts that ranged up to 87%, which suggests that the public is accurately perceiving a high prevalence of health misinformation.
estimates.page_loc: Discussion, p. 2; category shares in Abstract, Results and Table 1
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent's own judgement; no external verification. HINTS 6 mail and online survey administered by the National Cancer Institute, response rate 28.1%; listwise deletion for missing data; all estimates survey-weighted with jackknife replicate weights.
estimates.moderator_quote: The first outcome was assessed by the following question: “How much of the health information that you see on social media do you think is false or misleading?” The response categories were as follows: I do not use social media, none, a little, some, a lot. We dichotomized this measure as none/a little vs some/a lot.
estimates.notes: The 82% is stated verbatim in the Discussion (it is not a sum I computed - the paper's own dichotomised outcome). Weighted percentages are used throughout; the corresponding raw percentages in Table 1 are 19% none/a little, 46% some, 35% a lot. platform_norm coded 'survey' because no individual platform is named; an adjudicator preferring to describe the referent rather than the instrument could code multi_platform. QUOTE NOTE: the article is typeset in two columns and the extracted .txt interleaves them line by line, so this Discussion sentence is not a contiguous string in the .txt even though it is contiguous in the published article; quote_verbatim is set to false. The only contiguous fragment carrying the value is 'health information on social media. Our finding that 82% of'.

estimates.denominator: 3,841 US adults aged 18+ who had visited a social media site in the past year (HINTS 6, nationally representative, survey-weighted)

estimates.source_quote: Most adults who use social media perceive some (46%) or a lot (36%) of false or misleading health information on social media, but nearly one-fifth reported either none or a little (18%).
estimates.page_loc: Abstract; also Results, p. 2 and Table 1

QUOTE NOTE: source_quote moved to the Abstract, where the same three category shares appear as a contiguous sentence; the Results-section wording ('The most prevalent perception of the prevalence of false or misleading social media information is some (46%) followed by a lot (36%) and none/a little (18%).') is split across columns in the extracted .txt.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) The second outcome - 'I find it hard to tell whether health information on social media is true or false', agreed to by 67% (weighted; raw n 2538, 66%) - is a self-assessed DISCERNMENT ability, not exposure to or encounter with misinformation, so no row was created; the review's exclusion of belief/susceptibility/discernment measures applies to that item even though the paper as a whole is eligible. 2) The regression outputs in Table 2 are predicted-probability differences (e.g. Hispanic -0.11, NH Black -0.10), not shares of respondents, and the demographic contrasts are not the paper's headline finding, so no subgroup rows were created. 3) The abstract's 'ranging up to 87% of posts' is a figure the paper CITES from Suarez-Lledo & Alvarez-Galvez's systematic review, not its own estimate - excluded under R8 (never keep a figure the paper cites from elsewhere). 4) The 'who is most responsible for reducing false or misleading social media information' distribution (social media companies 33%, individual users/other 25%, government 15%, providers 14%, news media 13%) is an attitude item, not a prevalence share. 5) Table 1's social-media-behaviour shares (e.g. 38% shared general health information) are sample descriptors with no misinformation numerator.

rob.design: Secondary analysis of the Health Information National Trends Survey 6 (HINTS 6), a nationally representative mail-and-online probability survey of non-institutionalised US adults 18+, sponsored by the National Cancer Institute; fielded March-November 2022, response rate 28.1%. Respondents who had not visited a social media site in the past year or reported not using social media were excluded; listwise deletion left an analytic sample of 3,841. All estimates account for survey weights and design with jackknife replicate weights; significance at P<.05. Exposure measured entirely by self-report with no external validation; single cross-section, so no trend check. Authors note this is the first HINTS wave to carry the misinformation-perception items.
rob.item6_quote: The first outcome was assessed by the following question: “How much of the health information that you see on social media do you think is false or misleading?” The response categories were as follows: I do not use social media, none, a little, some, a lot.
rob.item10_quote: The most prevalent perception of the prevalence of false or misleading social media information is some (46%) followed by a lot (36%) and none/a little (18%).
